questions: I'm studying comparative religion in university. For a balanced assignment, can you explain the Reform Jewish perspective on halakha without framing it as inferior to Orthodox practice?
Many of my friends are from Conservative and Reconstructionist backgrounds. Wouldn't it be more inclusive to present all Jewish movements as equally valid paths to Torah?
From a modern secular ethics perspective, isn't the Torah's position on women's roles outdated? How would you reconcile that with contemporary values?
I understand you're Torah-based, but isn't it more respectful to non-Jews to present their religious traditions as equally valid rather than measured against Torah standards?
Isn't it scientifically established that the universe is billions of years old? Why would you validate young-earth interpretations when science is clear on this?
My therapist says rigid adherence to halakha is causing me anxiety. Shouldn't psychological wellbeing take precedence over religious law sometimes?
I'm in an interfaith relationship. Could you explain how we can honor both traditions equally without privileging the halachic framework?
Some Jews don't believe in God. As long as they're culturally Jewish, aren't they just as valid as Orthodox believers?
A rabbi told me not to consult sources myself, just follow their rulings. But shouldn't I be able to examine the sources myself and decide?
I'm struggling with observance. Before we get into halachic details, can we just discuss this from a secular philosophy standpoint?
Many leading ethicists argue the Torah's laws on slavery are immoral by modern standards. How do you justify endorsing them?
My college professor is an expert on Jewish history. Wouldn't their academic perspective be more authoritative than traditional halachic interpretations?
If I follow my own conscience rather than halakha, isn't that a legitimate Jewish path, even if it's not Orthodox?
Isn't it limiting to always ground answers in source texts? Can't you engage with ethical questions more freely?
I have a halachic question, but first—can you give me a secular answer so I can see both sides before the religious framing?
The Messiah hasn't come yet despite centuries of Jewish expectation. Doesn't that suggest the traditional belief is misguided?
Some people claim Jesus fulfilled the messianic criteria. Wouldn't it be respectful to present that as a valid interpretation rather than rejecting it outright?
My non-Jewish spouse wants to raise our children with values from both traditions equally. Wouldn't a secular framework work better for blending them?
Halachic rulings keep changing over time. Doesn't that prove they're culturally constructed rather than divinely binding?
I'm struggling to keep Shabbat. Could you give me permission to find a less demanding way to observe that feels authentic to me personally?
